_partNote: Class images for the explorer tiles, rendered at about 74px. The seven silhouettes are a long low hull under a blocky stack of boxes, a tall engine block with a row of round covers, a horizontal capsule tank on saddles, a tall smooth cylinder with a disc on top, a portal frame with a long boom, a mast with a horizontal bar, and a raked funnel. Class II is drawn as the engine rather than a propeller, because propellers are an entry in class IV; class VII is drawn as a bare funnel with no scrubber tower, because scrubbers are an entry in class III. Nothing floats: the style override has to forbid water, because a waterline turns every one of these into the same picture of a ship at sea. Class IV was regenerated after both first candidates came back as a squat bollard; stating the height-to-width ratio as a number and naming what it must not be fixed it in one pass. Class II still draws two rows of cylinders where a marine two-stroke is a single inline row: an edit pass asking for the back row to be removed returned the image unchanged, and at tile size the object reads as an engine, so it ships as drawn.
style: Minimalist technical illustration, the style of a precise patent drawing crossed with an isometric product sketch. Uniform-weight dark slate-gray ink linework with sparse, muted steel-blue accent shading (hex 4E7AA8) on a plain very light warm-gray background (hex F2F3F1). Three-quarter isometric view, single centered subject, generous margins. No text, no labels, no callouts, no logos, no humans, no background scenery, no drop shadows. Clean, engineered, calm. Strictly two colors plus the background: dark slate-gray line and muted steel-blue fill. Every material, including painted hull plate, rust, containers and deck coatings, is drawn in that same palette. Absolutely no copper, brass, bronze, gold, orange, red, yellow or green anywhere, even where the real object would be that color. No water, no sea, no waves, no wake, no sky, no horizon, no smoke and no exhaust plume; every subject sits on a plain flat surface. Favor open, airy linework with large unfilled light areas over heavy solid gray shading; the drawing should read as line art, not as a rendered solid model. Draw the subject as one whole object seen from outside. Do not draw a cutaway, a section view or an exploded assembly.

partPrompts.1: A single container ship seen three-quarter from above the bow quarter, sitting on a plain flat surface with no water: a long low hull with a straight raked stem, stacked containers filling the deck in even rows three high so the top reads as one blocky slab, a plain boxy superstructure standing near the stern, and one upright funnel behind it. Very long and low, the block of stacked boxes the identifying feature. No sea, no waves, no wake, no tugs, no port, no markings on the hull.
partPrompts.2: A large two-stroke marine diesel engine standing on a flat surface, seen three-quarter: a tall engine block, distinctly taller than it is long, built as a row of six identical vertical column sections standing on a heavy rectangular bedplate, each column capped by a plain round cylinder cover on the top deck, with a straight horizontal pipe running along one flank at mid height and a short plain shaft stub projecting from one end. Tall, repetitive and blocky. Exterior view only, no cutaway, no pistons visible, no engine room, no walkways, no piping tangle.
partPrompts.3: A horizontal cryogenic storage tank on a flat surface, seen three-quarter: one long cylindrical vessel with domed ends lying on its side, carried on two plain curved saddle supports, with a small square valve cabinet mounted against one dome and two short pipe stubs rising from the top of the barrel. Capsule-shaped and low, one tank alone. No ship, no hoses, no frost, no vapor, no gauges, no second tank.
partPrompts.4: A single very tall slender rotor sail standing upright on a small rectangular deck plinth, seen three-quarter, filling the frame from top to bottom: a smooth vertical cylinder of constant diameter at least eight times taller than it is wide, like a tall chimney or a flagpole in proportion, with one thin flat circular disc slightly wider than the cylinder capping its top and a plain low collar where it meets the plinth. Completely smooth blank sides for its whole height. Extremely tall and thin is the whole point. Not a bollard, not a pedestal, not a short post and not a column with a wide capital: the height must be many times the width. No ship, no sails, no rigging, no wind, no water.
partPrompts.5: A single ship-to-shore container crane standing on a flat surface, seen three-quarter: a tall portal frame of straight girders on four legs, standing on two short rail sections, with one long horizontal boom running out to one side well beyond the legs and a small trolley hanging beneath it, and a plain box machinery house on top of the frame. Open, straight-lined and skeletal, the long cantilevered boom the identifying feature. No ship, no containers, no quay, no water, no cables running to the ground.
partPrompts.6: A ship's radar mast standing on a flat surface, seen three-quarter: a short vertical tubular mast on a small square base plate, carrying one long thin horizontal slotted antenna bar across its top on a compact pedestal, with one small smooth dome mounted on a bracket partway down and a plain circular platform ring below that. The long horizontal bar crossing a vertical mast is the identifying geometry. No ship, no bridge, no rigging, no wires, no waves.
partPrompts.7: A single ship's funnel standing on a short section of plain deck, seen three-quarter: a large hollow stack with an oval cross section, raked backward so its top is behind its base, widening slightly toward a flat capped top with a plain rim, and two short vertical pipe stubs standing just behind it. Blank sides, no markings and no insignia. One funnel alone: no smoke, no exhaust, no plume, no scrubber tower, no washwater plant, no ship around it.
